column1: What physical principle causes a DC brushed motor to produce rotational torque?
column2: The Lorentz force: current flowing through a coil inside a magnetic field generates a force perpendicular to both the current and the field, producing torque on the armature.

column1: In a brushed DC motor, what role do the brushes and commutator play, and what cost does this introduce?
column2: Brushes (carbon contacts) maintain electrical continuity to the rotating coil via a segmented commutator ring, sustaining rotation—but this introduces resistive heat loss, mechanical wear, and electromagnetic noise.

column1: What are the two extreme operating points on a DC motor's torque-speed curve, and what characterizes each?
column2: Stall torque: shaft is locked, current draw and torque are maximum, speed is zero. Free-run speed: shaft is unloaded, speed is maximum, torque output is near zero. All real operation lies linearly between these extremes.

column1: What is the gear ratio formula, and what does R>1 vs R<1 mean physically?
column2: R = N_driven / N_driver. R>1 = reduction (driven shaft slower, torque multiplied by R). R<1 = overdrive (driven shaft faster, torque divided by R).

column1: Calculate the gear ratio and torque multiplication for an 8-tooth driver meshing with a 40-tooth driven gear.
column2: R = 40/8 = 5. Five input turns produce one output turn, and output torque is multiplied 5x (before friction losses).

column1: What is the fundamental invariant linking torque, angular velocity, and power through an ideal gear mesh?
column2: P = τ·ω (power = torque × angular velocity) is conserved through an ideal gear mesh; only the distribution between torque and speed changes, not the total power.

column1: Why do real Lego gear trains fail to achieve the ideal power conservation predicted by P = τ·ω?
column2: Friction losses from gear mesh contact, axle bending under load, and microscopic gear tooth deformation cause real systems to fall short of the ideal, each stage typically losing 2-5% of power.

column1: Why is a worm gear stage uniquely costly in terms of power transmission efficiency compared to standard spur gear meshes?
column2: A single worm-to-wheel mesh can consume 40-60% of input power, far more than the 2-5% loss typical of a standard gear stage, due to the sliding (rather than rolling) contact inherent to worm gear engagement.

column1: What is the 'efficiency valley' a drivetrain designer must target when matching motor to mechanical load?
column2: The operating zone between two failure modes: over-gearing (motor runs near stall torque, generating heat and gear stress) and under-gearing (motor spins freely but lacks torque/grunt under load).

column1: What key feature distinguishes the Control+ Large Angular Motor from the standard XL Motor in Lego Technic?
column2: The Control+ Large Angular Motor adds absolute position feedback (critical for steering/suspension control), while its peak torque is similar to the XL Motor.

column1: What is the fundamental invariant (closed-loop architecture) governing all motorized Lego control systems like SPIKE Prime or EV3?
column2: The feedback loop: continuously sensing state, comparing it against a target setpoint, calculating the error term, and issuing corrective motor commands—enabling position holding, velocity regulation, and multi-motor synchronization.

column1: In PWM motor control, what does duty cycle determine, and how is motor direction controlled?
column2: Duty cycle determines the average voltage delivered to the motor (e.g., 50% duty = half supply voltage, 100% = full battery voltage); direction is controlled by inverting the polarity of the MOSFET H-bridge, reversing current flow.
